Case 2: Assume p is a prime number not in the set {2, 5}.
Define Eduardo's first move: choose i = (p - 1) and a(p - 1) = 0.
By Fermat's Little Theorem, (10^(p-1)) ≡ 1 (mod p).
Define d = (p - 1)/2. Then d is a natural number.
We have (10^d)^2 = 10^(p-1) ≡ 1 (mod p).

Since p is prime, p divides ((10^d) + 1) or p divides ((10^d) - 1).

Define a strategy for Eduardo:
After Fernando chooses an index i and a value a(i), Eduardo responds as follows:
If 0 ≤ i ≤ (d - 1), define j = i + d.
If d ≤ i ≤ (p - 2), define j = i - d.
In both cases, Eduardo chooses index j and sets a(j) = a(i).
We have 10^j ≡ -10^i (mod p) because:
If j = i + d, then 10^j = 10^(i+d) = (10^i)*(10^d) ≡ (10^i)*(-1) = -10^i (mod p).
If j = i - d, then 10^j = 10^(i-d) = (10^i)/(10^d). Since 10^d ≡ -1 (mod p), we have 10^j ≡ (10^i)/(-1) = -10^i (mod p).

Therefore, after Eduardo's response, the sum for the pair {i, j} is a(i)*10^i + a(j)*10^j ≡ 0 (mod p).
The pairing of indices is possible because the set I \ {(p-1)} can be partitioned into pairs {r, r+d} for r in {0, 1, ..., (d-1)}.
Since Eduardo's first move was index (p-1) with value 0, and he always responds immediately to Fernando's move by taking the paired index, Eduardo can always maintain that the sum of all chosen terms is divisible by p.

After Fernando chooses an index i and a value a(i), Eduardo responds as follows:
If 0 ≤ i ≤ (d - 1), define j = i + d.
If d ≤ i ≤ (p - 2), define j = i - d.
In both cases, Eduardo chooses index j and sets a(j) = 9 - a(i).
We have 10^j ≡ 10^i (mod p) because:
